input.title: Content-hash gating avoids paying for redundant AI extraction

input.description: Source systems fire document-updated events for metadata-only changes like tags and titles, so hashing the OCR text and skipping extraction when it is unchanged removes most repeat LLM cost.

input.content:
In a document-sync pipeline the expensive step is the model call: extracting structured fields from OCR text costs real money per document, and unlike the rest of the pipeline that cost does not amortise.

The trap is that "document updated" from a source system does not mean "the document's content changed". In Paperless-ngx, a Document Updated event fires when someone adds a tag, renames the document, changes its correspondent or moves its storage location. None of those change a single character of the OCR text the extractor reads. A pipeline that reacts to the event by re-extracting pays the full model cost for an input it has already processed, and — because model output is not deterministic — may also produce a slightly different answer, generating a spurious update downstream.

The fix is to hash the extractor's actual input, not the event: store the hash of the OCR text alongside the extraction result, and on each event compare the incoming text's hash against the stored one. Equal hash means the extractor's input is unchanged, so the previous result still stands and the model call is skipped entirely. Metadata-only edits — which are the majority of update events in a system where humans curate tags — then cost nothing.

Note what the hash is taken over: it must cover exactly the bytes fed to the model. Hashing a whole API payload would include the metadata that just changed and defeat the purpose; hashing a document ID or modification timestamp would never match. The gate works only when its key is the extractor's input.

## Methodology grounding

This is compare-before-acting from [[idempotent maintenance operations are safe to automate because running them twice produces the same result as running them once]], with a specific reason for wanting it: the operation being made repeat-safe is expensive and non-deterministic, so the cost of running it twice is both a bill and a spurious diff, not merely a wasted cycle.
